---
title: "Hands-on: Sparse Matrices for Large Networks"
---

A dense adjacency matrix for Earth's 8 billion people would need 512 exabytes. Real networks are sparse, and this notebook is about exploiting that.

## The idea in one page

Storing an adjacency matrix as a full table wastes almost all of it: a real network has a handful of edges per node, so nearly every entry is zero. The fix is to write down only the entries that are not zero.

Start from an **adjacency list** — for each row of the matrix, the column IDs that carry a value, and the values themselves:

$$
\{\text{Row ID}: (\text{Column ID}, \text{Value})\}
$$

**Compressed Sparse Row (CSR)** is nothing more than this list flattened into three plain arrays:

| Array | What it holds |
| :--- | :--- |
| `indices` | the column IDs of every non-zero entry, row after row |
| `data` | the matching values, in the same order |
| `indptr` | where each row *starts* inside those two arrays |

`indptr` is the only one that needs a moment's thought. It is the running total of how many entries each row contributed, beginning at 0 — so `indptr[i]` is the position in `indices` where row $i$ begins, and `indptr[i+1]` is where it ends. Row 0 occupies positions `0 … indptr[1]-1`, row 1 picks up at `indptr[1]`, and so on.

Once you see that, two network operations become one-liners that need no library at all:

- **Degree of node $i$**: `indptr[i+1] - indptr[i]` — the number of non-zero entries in row $i$.
- **Neighbours of node $i$**: `indices[indptr[i]:indptr[i+1]]` — the column IDs in row $i$, which are exactly the nodes $i$ connects to. The matching edge weights are `data[indptr[i]:indptr[i+1]]`.

This is why CSR is the format every network library reaches for: the operation you perform most often — "give me this node's neighbours" — is a contiguous slice.

Now go and build it.

## What you will build

1. Construct a CSR matrix from an edge list with `scipy.sparse`.
2. Take the format apart and read `data`, `indices` and `indptr` directly.
3. Recover a node's degree and its neighbour list straight from `indptr` and `indices`, without any library call.
4. Measure the memory a dense array and a CSR matrix need for the same network, as the network grows.
5. Use sparse matrix-vector products to run the component-finding code from earlier in the module at a scale where dense arrays would not fit.

## What to watch for

- Plot memory against network size for both formats. The curves diverge faster than intuition suggests: dense storage grows as $N^2$ while CSR grows as $O(M + N)$.
- CSR is fast for row-based operations and matrix-vector products, and slow at repeatedly reading single entries. Time both and you will remember which is which.
- Compare CSR against COO and CSC on the same operations. The right format depends entirely on what you are about to do with the matrix.
